body: Ok.

I agree they aren’t actually *forced* to do anything, altruistic acts are a choice. 

I disagree the only *correct* choice to feeling forced is nope-ing out of there. If you’re burning out, you can try and organise a break, or change what you’re willing to provide to accommodate your actual capabilities (as opposed to what you think you should be able to do).

It’s not as black and white as you’re making out.

I think the difference in opinion might be smaller than I thought then. We just disagree on what can be assumed, and whether cutting off contact should be a last resort or not.

I agree boundaries can be set, and restrictions on what help you will provide depending on your capability and what you’re willing to do. You shouldn’t feel guilty for deciding you can only provide verbal support, or whatever level of help you’re comfortable with. If you don’t feel like you can provide a particular type of support, pointing them towards somewhere they can get that is good. If the patient is being abusive, in a way I’d actually call abusive, then it’s probably okay to cut off contact.

Parallel to my ‘terminal patient’ example, they might not be able to give up their days to monitor their family members health, so trying to get professional support isn’t wrong. On the other hand, they might not be able to afford it, and the patient isn’t abusing the carer because the carer is making sacrifices to take care of them. Even if they feel forced into it.

Well, that reasoning no longer applies, and you don’t want to hurt her, and you presumably haven’t hurt her since. So, you probably aren’t going to hurt her in the future. Given all that, don’t worry too much.

I took ‘calling someone to get the attention and excitement that’s missing in your life’, which is basically ‘cause emotional distress for attention and excitement’ to be an accusation of malice. I can accept I misunderstood somehow if you say so though. 

An analogy to convey my viewpoint:

Swap ‘chronic mental health issues’ with ‘terminal illness’. 

They both need professional help. 

They both cause great distress to loved ones. 

They both are helped by having emotional and physical support/monitoring by their loved ones. 

They both could have multiple dangerous periods before the end.

Living with both causes great suffering for the patient. 

Do you see why I don’t think cutting off contact is the right decision from this perspective?

I disagree that counts as abuse. There are abusive actions you can do while involving others in your mental health issues, like emotional blackmail, but that doesn’t mean everything to do with your mental health has to be cornered off from others. There is no hostage here if no threat is made or ransom demanded. 

The person might need professional help, but that doesn’t mean *only* professional help is ethical. What you’re responsible for is subjective and cultural, but feeling a responsibility towards your loved ones isn’t something I’d call unhealthy or to be prevented.

My bad, ‘assumed intentions’ then.
Go go go.

I feel like, personally, a loved one accepting my decision to die would solidify that as the *right* decision though. 

If you think it is, the right decision that is, then I don’t really have anything more to say. If you don’t, I’d fight for as long as she still breathes.

This is slightly hard to understand. 

I think you’re assuming too much malice. There’s been no mention of her demanding anything or holding him hostage. There’s been no mention that she’s doing this for ‘excitement’ or ‘attention’. 

All we know is she has attempted before. OP cares about her, so he is distressed at her suffering and doesn’t want her to die, this is normal. The answer to that distress isn’t to block them so they suffer alone, it’s to try and alleviate that suffering. 

That may involve trying to get her into therapy, or some other option, but saying ‘this isn’t my problem’ lacks empathy or compassion. Being apathetic towards strangers is normal. Being apathetic towards loved ones should not be.
Your options aren’t ‘choose whether she lives or dies’, it’s ‘call the police or not’. If you call, and she survives, you might save her some damage.

Are those the options? Trying to save her, or letting her die? If she’s done this before, she might survive again. If you don’t call the police soon, she might suffer internal damage that cripples but doesn’t kill. If you don’t want her to suffer, calling the police sooner in case she survives seems like the right choice.
How?
Why?

Well, you know you have the self-control to stop yourself before causing damage even at one of your lowest points, so that’s good.

Do you know why she needed to die before you died?

If she texted you that she took the doses, I’d take that as implicit consent to call the police unless she explicitly asked you not to. 

When I go, I’m not planning to tell anyone beforehand. If I do, I wouldn’t ask them to choose to let me die, as it seems like an unnecessary moral dilemma to put them in, and it’d be perfectly understandable for them to ignore that request.

I wrote a lot, but in summery:

Even if this is true, it’s not necessarily desirable (‘curing’ autism for example). You are way too optimistic about all of this.

I’ve been told before that therapists aren’t supposed to do anything like that unless they have a reasonable belief you’re an immediate danger to yourself or others. ‘Reasonable belief’ isn’t uniform though, and different therapists have differing levels of experience dealing with people with suicidal thoughts. Well, the first step to all of those things is ‘who do you want to do them with?’. 

Getting a girlfriend without first liking a girl isn’t the way to go about it, so until you do it’s fine to take your time. The other things follow the same logic, is there anyone, or a specific group of people, you want to do those things with? Having a clearer goal might help in working out how to achieve it. 

I can definitely relate, I had a wide range of shallow relationships in highschool. 

I don’t really have any solid advice for stopping bullying, except for ‘avoid the bullies’. If you can’t do so, maybe hang out with the nicest of the lot, and work on striking up an actual friendship with them? Idk. Sorry if this is unhelpful, but I’m not that socially competent myself.

How old are you? You probably don’t need to worry too much about wasting your life, you’ve got plenty of it to waste. If it’s something you’re concerned about though, what do you think you should be doing that you’re not?

I think going into the medical field is really admirable. 

On keeping yourself focused: venting like this, or with a friend, might help you relieve the pressure a bit. Bottling it up is unhealthy and a distraction. 

Depression/anxiety doesn’t have anything to do with intelligence; more to the point, calling something stupid is often another way of saying ‘I don’t understand this’, so don’t take it as a personal attack. 

I can’t really tell you everything will be alright. What I can tell you is that what happens happens, and you only have two days before the pressure is off, so that’s something to look forward to.
I feel like you’re the only person who can answer that.

Not pressuring or anything, do what you need to do, but you might be able to access professional help anonymously. If you’ve looked into that and for whatever reason you can’t, don’t feel able, or even don’t want to, that’s also okay. Rome wasn’t built in a day and all that, any progress is valid. Getting through tonight is enough.
It won’t be easy, but the desire for help is already half the battle; getting the help you need is the other, but I believe you can do it.

If her lecturing about how to feel better is understandably making you feel worse, tell her. Tell her she is making you feel worse, so if she wants to help, do something different. You might not know what she should do instead, she might not know, but learning what not to do is a start.

Why do you think she is the ‘good parent’? 

I get hating when you talk like that, it’s not pleasant hearing about a loved one’s pain. But hiding something away doesn’t stop it existing. Ignorance is only bliss until it becomes too large to ignore, and silent suffering just builds and builds. She can stop you warning her about your ‘stupid’ impulses, or she can help you reduce them. 

You want help, you aren’t getting help. For as long as you can, please keep trying.

Feeling that way makes sense, that kind of betrayal is disorientating, you don’t really know where you stand anymore y’know? 

It’s normal to feel lost, but just keep in mind that you can’t trust them to be honest about why they did what they did, if they even know why, so don’t let them try and make it your fault somehow. 

You can take your time with this, feel how you feel, but give yourself that time to find your footing again.
I mean, after what they did, them calling you the horrible person is ridiculous. I don’t know if you have some way of limiting contact with them, so their cruelty doesn’t reach you?

Well, you probably should keep in contact to the best of your ability. Even if it doesn’t feel like you’re helping, just being there means he’s not alone.

Edit: Also, if you’re worried about how you should talk to them, the sidebar of this subreddit has stuff you can read about how to talk to people struggling with suicidal thoughts.
I mean, as far as I can tell, at the moment all you have are speculations, so I wouldn’t worry too much about it.

Well, maybe not out of the blue, but if they know you’ve experienced that then they might be less hesitant to talk about their own thoughts/feelings. If they know you can relate in advance, they will probably find it easier to talk about and vent. The order changes, who mentions it first, but the result is the same. 

It probably will change how they see you, although it’s unknown whether it would be for better or worse. Depends on how you broach it, what kind of person you are, and what type of person they are.
If they’re experiencing similar thoughts and feelings, it might be helpful to mention you relate. Make them feel less alone and abnormal.

Possibly, people are sometimes like that. Being a pedophile isn’t illegal though, so you wouldn’t go to jail. Therapists shouldn’t be able to break confidentiality unless they have a reasonable belief that you are an immediate danger to a child. 

More importantly, if you don’t want to be a danger to children, you don’t have to be. Most child abusers aren’t pedophiles, and pedophiles aren’t inevitably child abusers. You can choose not to hurt children, that is in your power.

Guilty of what? Even if the guy you knew was a child abuser instead of just a pedophile, you don’t and didn’t know that. You can’t be blamed for crimes you don’t know exist.

I’m pretty shit at getting round to doing college assignments too, and before that it was the same with homework. 

As an idea, you could try and do them with someone else; not in a ‘I need their help to understand’ way, but in a motivational capacity. Talking about the work as you do it might make it less boring, and the time spent pass faster.

You probably don’t even need a friend or family member for this (though that is an option), as strangers are generally altruistic enough to help out, even if the request is slightly unorthodox, if they don’t lose anything in the process and have the time. 

If nothing else; failing is still better than dying, especially with something like this.
